title: Waking at amrit vela
hookLine: the day starts early, in the quiet before dawn
tomorrow: what does water have to do with prayer?

lines: NOT TO GET AHEAD. TO GET THERE FIRST.
cards: Phones have a mode for the end of the night: wind down, the screen goes gray, notifications hush. The Gurus named the other end of the night.
Amrit vela, the ambrosial hours, the quiet before dawn, before the group chat wakes up and the day starts asking for things. So the alarm goes off in the dark, on purpose. Not to get ahead of anyone.

teach.b: Japji names it, in its fourth pauri. In paraphrase: in the ambrosial hours, reflect on the true Name and its greatness. And Guru Ram Das, on ang 305, sketches a Sikh's morning.
In paraphrase: whoever calls himself a Sikh of the True Guru rises early and meditates on the Lord's Name; makes the effort in the early morning, bathes, and dips in the pool of nectar.

teach.h: ONE VIEW: HOLD TO THE HOUR.
teach.b: Now, two views Sikhs hold about that hour. One says: hold to the hour. The Gurus named the early morning, before light, and the hour itself does something.
The house is still, the mind hasn't filled up yet, and getting up in the dark is part of the offering. Move it to whenever suits you, and it stops being amrit vela.
The other says: hold to the first. Think of a nurse coming off a night shift, a new parent, a driver who parks at sunrise.

For them, this view says, what the Gurus guard is the Name before the world rushes in, and the early morning is where that usually happens in an ordinary life, not the only place it can. Both views keep the same center.
The Name comes first. They differ on whether the clock is part of the gift.

how: Sikhs who keep amrit vela rise in the hours before dawn, bathe, and spend amrit vela in simran and the morning banis; gurdwaras hold early services, and people whose work runs through the night look for their own quiet first hour.

games.q: what does “waking at amrit vela” mean?
o: the last prayer of the night, said before sleep
the quiet hours before dawn, kept for the Name
a fast kept from sunrise until the evening prayer

games.q: the early hour — tap the pairs.
p: reflect on the true Name then
a Sikh of the Guru rises early
the Name before the world rushes in

s: amrit vela is about getting a head start on work
Japji keeps the hour for the true Name and its greatness.
Guru Ram Das describes a Sikh rising early to meditate on the Name
ang 305: rising early, bathing, the Name.
Sikhs all agree the hour itself can't move
some hold to the hour; others, thinking of night workers, hold to the Name first.

games.q: your dad drives overnight runs this week and says his amrit vela is when he parks at sunrise. you hold to the hours before dawn. before you argue, what's his best case?
o: the Gurus guard the Name before the world rushes in; for a night driver, that's after he parks.
the hymns never mention any time of day, so every hour is exactly the same.
the early hour is only meant for Sikhs who've taken amrit, so he can choose.
games.why: that's the strongest version of the second view. Japji does name the ambrosial hours, so the first view has a real case too: the clock may be part of the gift.

practice: Set tomorrow's alarm fifteen minutes earlier, now, while the idea is fresh. Then sit with one question: what's most likely to stop me, and what will I do when it does? Keep the answer small enough to keep.

wordCard.voice: Waking at amrit vela. The ambrosial hours before dawn, kept for the true Name and its greatness.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: amrit vela, the ambrosial hours, named in Japji's fourth pauri.

carryVoice: Carry this: the early hour, whatever the clock says, because the Name gets there first. See you in the morning.

sources.ref: Ang 2 (Japji, pauri 4: amrit vela sach naau vadiaaee veechaar), paraphrased
Ang 305 (Gauri ki Var, Mahala 4: gur satgur kaa jo sikh akhaae, su bhalke uth har naam dhiaavai; udam kare bhalke parbhaatee isnaan kare amrit sar naavai), paraphrased
